title: Ang 831–848: ashtpadis and the days
tomorrow: when is singing Bilaval actually worth it?

cards: Open a calendar app and every day already has a job: practice Monday, a shift on Thursday, family on Sunday. Guru Amar Das wrote a calendar too, on ang 841. Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, all seven.
And every one of them, whatever else it holds, points back to the same One.

teach.b: These pages hold Bilaval's longer hymns. First ashtpadis, hymns of eight stanzas.
Then Guru Nanak's Thiti, a poem on the lunar days of the month. Then Guru Amar Das's Var Sat, the seven days of the week. His Sunday, in paraphrase: the Primal Being is He, there is no other.
And each day after makes the same move: a weekday's name, then the One. No day is luckier. No day is left out.
Now hold this week up to the light. Faithful, moved off the funeral fire and into each morning. Farid's raft, built while the water's calm.
Morning joy, in words too small to fit. Joy that comes through the singing. A line drawn all around, and the hot wind outside it.
And the ninth Guru, where help reaches when love can't.
Six days, and each one fit inside Guru Amar Das's calendar: a day of the week, pointing back.

how: Guru Nanak's Thiti (ang 838) and Guru Amar Das's Var Sat (ang 841) are read and sung as part of Bilaval; they use the calendar to turn the mind back to the One.

games.q: you dread mondays so much that every sunday night is ruined. what does Guru Amar Das's seven days have to say?
o: monday points back to the One too; it's not just the day before a bad one.
sunday is the holy day, so monday doesn't really count.
push through; the poem says days are an illusion anyway.
games.why: every weekday in Var Sat gets its name and then the One. none is left out, none is only a step toward another.

practice: Close your eyes and say today's weekday quietly to yourself, once. Then let it go, and sit in the stillness for the rest of the time, as if this day had no other job. If you'd like, read ang 838 first.
